I live in Toronto now and don't use Hydro Ottawa. But I think their billing practices are alarming and want to warn other consumers.

I used to live in an apartment downtown for a year. I moved in with my parents to do a masters, cancelled my account. Paid off everything and formally closed it. But for more than a year, it kept taking money from a different account of mine. At random times. I called their customer service many times. Sent them proof of withdrawals. They would say no, my account is closed. No debits are happening.

But when my parents and I went through our bills, it turned out that they had linked my banking info to my parents' billing number, because I told them I was moving in with my parents. But my parents didn't notice because they always get refunds of overpayments. So they thought it was normal. After many hours on the phone, multiple reps, and finally a manager actually investigated. Confirmed the mistake and fixed it. But they refused to refund at first. Just apologized.

I don't give my banking details to them for auto-debit again. Their approach with our data is just reckless. It should worry everyone.

I agree with Misti Y--. Some people will love the Cirque shows and not really like Le Reve. This is a separate discussion. For me the theatre is the best part. The design and the decor is simply stunning from beginning to end. The concept behind the show is really beautiful and appealing. It doesn't translate to the actual show very well. The story isn't that entertaining. On the show that I saw, the stage kept breaking down all night. It was hard to stay engaged in it, even during the impressive scenes. Le Reve tries to reach for the flashiness and spectacle of Cirque, but never really achieves it. It's mostly for the chance to go see the beautiful theatre. Otherwise you might be better off putting your money into another show.

It's a float valve connecting troughs to a pressurised water line. Usually there's a float, a plastic ball or block. It floats on the water and is connected to the lever arm. So when the cows drink, the water level drops, the float sinks, the lever arm tips and it pulls the plunger, washer, whatever, away from the seat. So it opens and the water flows into the trough. As it fills, the float lifts. So it pushes the plunger back, closes the seat, and the opening gets smaller and smaller. And then it closes. When it starts to overflow, it's usually a worn or dirty washer. Or the float is punctured or waterlogged, so it's not lifting enough to close the valve. So it just keeps flowing and overflows.

Apple deserves a mention, from personal experience. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high schoolers. They cost about twice as much as alternatives and would break like once a month. I never dropped my laptop. But I changed the hard drive 5 times in 4 years and reinstalled the OS many times. A friend's MacBook Pro even caught fire while he was watching a movie, smoke alarm went off. And Apple support never diagnosed anything. They would just back up the computer, wipe it and restore files. Same with iPhones. I had the first iPhone and it would malfunction constantly. Now Apple puts out a new iPhone every 2 months or so, only the camera is slightly better. I'll only give them credit for iPads, which are the best tablets right now, but Android tablets might catch up.

I was brought to Vegas all the time. I saw a lot of shows before I turned 21. I have an idea of what these productions can be. Its fine, but not a must see in Vegas. I would not build a trip around it. The circular stage is really clever. From almost any seat, you get a decent view. That is rare in these big shows. If you stay at the Wynn or Encore, you can get tickets for 99. Normally they cost 125. I think the individual acts are really good. The performers are strong. Aerialists and acrobats, etc. But I have seen these things done as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. The story is unclear. It is not there. I do not really understand what it is trying to say. There is too much going on. Too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many attempts to wow. I think less would be more. But with the few cool stunts aside, it was just a regular show. I was not blown away. The people I was with did not seem to be overwhelmed. Some of my friends did enjoy it, so if you have never seen it, go. Especially if you get the Wynn and Encore deal. But I would not see it again or pay full price a second time. It tries to be this stereotypical big flashy Vegas show where more is better. But to me, more was just messier.

The College Board is just hypocritical. A friend took the one hour Subject Test, but the proctor accidentally gave the room about twenty extra minutes. She is honest, and she knew that would make the test less standardized. So she called the hotline to report it.
The result was pure institutional injustice. After their "investigation" they said there wasn't enough evidence to blame the proctor or the other students. But then they did find enough evidence to blame my friend, and her scores were voided. Punishing the person who honestly reported the problem and excusing the actual violator? That is how messed up they are.

Bought a skateboard at Zumiez, then went back for the rest of my stuff. At first it felt good. My friend, his little brother, and I sat with a lady who introduced herself as a manager. She said she'd been putting boards together every day she worked there, and that on her bad days she'd snapped at customers. I thought it would be quick. Fifteen minutes, at most. But it took ninety. She ruined two bolts, then swapped them for ones that looked like they might be sold to someone else. She finally got her brother and another guy - another manager apparently - to help finish it off. No apology. They've lost our future business. It really broke my heart.

Its a bakery at 3:17 AM, the mixer is just humming, really loud, vibration goes through my boots. Its dark and flour dust is all over the air, catching the fluorescent light, looks like snow hanging there. The sourdough loaves are on wooden boards, still pale soft, not done with the final bake. I wipe my hands on the apron. Its stiff, dried dough and sweat. I move to the counter to check the lock. Its not needed really, just paranoid, a ritual.
There it was. The History of Salt, hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. Every Thursday for six weeks its been there, put exactly on the glass display case, next to the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp, and we are not a branch of the municipal system, so where does it come from. I picked it up, felt cold. I opened it and expected blank pages or some forgotten bookmark. Instead a square of lined notebook paper folded up slipped out, hit the counter, soft tap. I unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. It said, You knead with your left hand dominant, stop favoring the right, it ruins the tension. I just stared at it. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. I look at my hands, red knuckled, dusted white. I closed the book. I put it back on the glass, aligned the spine perfectly with the edge. Then I turn off the overhead light above the display. Book is now in shadow.

Its possible to feel suffocated in a room even when its a comfortable temperature. This is because temperature is only one part of comfort. Humidity is the problem. When its high, it slows down evaporation of moisture from your skin. That makes the air feel heavy. Its also about airflow. If air is not moving, carbon dioxide and odors and heat just hang around. That makes the room feel stuffy. Air conditioning can cool the air but it does not mean it will reduce humidity or move the air. Opening a window or running a fan or ventilation can help. It moves the air and lowers the moisture.

Bought this mechanical keyboard second hand for 38 dollars and it has been a chaotic but decent ride. The seller communication was terrible. I asked about the switch type before buying and they took a week to respond with one word. By then I had already taken the gamble and ordered it. The board is well loved. The spacebar rattles like a loose Lego brick which is incredibly annoying, and the E key sometimes repeats so I get typos like theee instead of the. But despite the quirks I really love typing on it. The tactile feedback is fantastic and its really comfortable for hammering out long painful work emails. I considered shipping it back but returning a 38 dollar heavy slab of plastic was more hassle than it was worth. So I kept it and honestly I have grown fond of its flaws. If you don't mind a little DIY tuning and the occasional double typed letter its a budget win.

Old school attendance registers are pretty useful for reconstructing daily life. Historians use them to figure out who was there and who wasn't and how often, and sometimes why they missed. This helps you infer things like seasonal work demands, illness, bad weather, poverty or family stuff, migration, local emergencies. So you can see patterns by gender, age, neighborhood, social class. And how education fitted into work and household routines and community expectations. Across many years, you get changes in schooling habits and public health. But the thing is the registers only record what the school chose to note. They don't really go into what the kids experienced. Absences get misreported or are incomplete and teachers might have their own assumptions. So they're really only useful when you compare them to other sources.

I spent $38 on a used mechanical keyboard and got about $38 worth of keyboard, maybe a little more. Let me start with the flaws. The spacebar rattles, not a gentle click, a hollow loose clatter every time my thumb hits it, like you push a tray of cutlery. I stopped noticing it during the day but at night it sounds louder than it has any right to. The E key also repeats itself sometimes, so meeting becomes meeeeting. Happens maybe once every few paragraphs. So it's just often enough to make me proofread. Communication with the seller was slow. I asked what switches it was before buying, got a reply a week later. It was brown switches. Still, the surprise is that it's actually comfortable to type on. Cushioned feeling, I can write long emails without my wrists complaining. Which is more than I can say for the flat laptop keyboard I had. I thought about returning it but the hassle didn't seem worth it. So it stays on my desk. It rattles, repeats, and quietly earns its keep. Three stars.
